claim: ARL13B is a regulatory GTPase highly enriched in cilia.
source: ARL13B is a regulatory GTPase highly enriched in cilia.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Complete loss of Arl13b disrupts cilia architecture.
source: Complete loss of Arl13b disrupts cilia architecture, protein trafficking and Sonic hedgehog signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by prior published work cited in the manuscript.

claim: Complete loss of Arl13b disrupts protein trafficking.
source: Complete loss of Arl13b disrupts cilia architecture, protein trafficking and Sonic hedgehog signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by prior published work cited in the manuscript.

claim: Complete loss of Arl13b disrupts Sonic hedgehog signaling.
source: Complete loss of Arl13b disrupts cilia architecture, protein trafficking and Sonic hedgehog signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by prior published work cited in the manuscript.

claim: ARL13BV358A retains all known biochemical function.
source: To determine whether ARL13B is required within cilia, we knocked in a cilia-excluded variant of ARL13B (V358A) and showed it retains all known biochemical function.
evidence: This is demonstrated through GEF activity assays shown in Figure 1 and referenced prior work on GTP hydrolysis.

claim: ARL13BV358A protein was expressed but could not be detected in cilia.
source: We found that ARL13BV358A protein was expressed but could not be detected in cilia, even when retrograde ciliary transport was blocked.
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunofluorescence data in Figures 2 and 3, and western blot data in Figure 2D-E.

claim: ARL13BV358A protein could not be detected in cilia even when retrograde ciliary transport was blocked.
source: We found that ARL13BV358A protein was expressed but could not be detected in cilia, even when retrograde ciliary transport was blocked.
evidence: This is demonstrated through ciliobrevin-D treatment experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Arl13bV358A/V358A mice are viable.
source: We showed Arl13bV358A/V358A mice are viable and fertile with normal Shh signal transduction.
evidence: This is demonstrated by breeding data in Table 1 showing Mendelian ratios of offspring.

claim: Arl13bV358A/V358A mice are fertile.
source: We showed Arl13bV358A/V358A mice are viable and fertile with normal Shh signal transduction.
evidence: This is demonstrated by breeding data in Table 1 showing normal litter sizes from homozygous crosses.

claim: Arl13bV358A/V358A mice have normal Shh signal transduction.
source: We showed Arl13bV358A/V358A mice are viable and fertile with normal Shh signal transduction.
evidence: This is demonstrated by neural tube patterning data in Figure 4 showing normal expression of Shh-dependent markers.

claim: Arl13bV358A/V358A cells displayed short cilia.
source: However, in contrast to wild type cilia, Arl13bV358A/V358A cells displayed short cilia and lacked ciliary ARL3 and INPP5E.
evidence: This is demonstrated by cilia length measurements in Figure 6B.

claim: Arl13bV358A/V358A cells lacked ciliary ARL3.
source: However, in contrast to wild type cilia, Arl13bV358A/V358A cells displayed short cilia and lacked ciliary ARL3 and INPP5E.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5G.

claim: Arl13bV358A/V358A cells lacked ciliary INPP5E.
source: However, in contrast to wild type cilia, Arl13bV358A/V358A cells displayed short cilia and lacked ciliary ARL3 and INPP5E.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5H.

claim: ARL13B's role within cilia can be uncoupled from its function outside of cilia.
source: These data indicate that ARL13B's role within cilia can be uncoupled from its function outside of cilia.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ARL13BV358A, which is excluded from cilia, can rescue Shh signaling but not cilia length or ARL3/INPP5E localization.

claim: The cilia defects upon complete absence of ARL13B do not underlie the alterations in Shh transduction.
source: Furthermore, these data imply that the cilia defects upon complete absence of ARL13B do not underlie the alterations in Shh transduction, which is unexpected given the requirement of cilia for Shh transduction.
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that Arl13bV358A/V358A cells have short cilia but normal Shh signaling.

claim: The Hedgehog signaling pathway is essential for embryogenesis in a wide variety of organisms.
source: The Hedgehog (Hh) signaling pathway is essential for embryogenesis in a wide variety of organisms.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in developmental biology supported by extensive literature.

claim: The core components of the Hh pathway are conserved in vertebrates.
source: Initially discovered in Drosophila where there is a single Hh ligand, the core components of the Hh pathway are conserved in vertebrates (Nüsslein-Volhard and Wieschaus, 1980).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference and is established knowledge in the field.

claim: There are three Hh ligands in vertebrates: Sonic (Shh), Indian (Ihh) and Desert (Dhh).
source: There are three Hh ligands in vertebrates, Sonic (Shh), Indian (Ihh) and Desert (Dhh), that regulate a multitude of developmental processes including formation of the limbs and digits, the bones of the skull and face, and the patterning of the neural tube (Placzek and Briscoe, 2018).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by the cited reference.

claim: Diminished Hh signaling during embryogenesis results in birth defects.
source: Diminished Hh signaling during embryogenesis results in birth defects whereas increased Hh signaling leads to tumors, highlighting the importance of the pathway and its regulation (Raleigh and Reiter, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Increased Hh signaling leads to tumors.
source: Diminished Hh signaling during embryogenesis results in birth defects whereas increased Hh signaling leads to tumors, highlighting the importance of the pathway and its regulation (Raleigh and Reiter, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Primary cilia are required for vertebrate Hh signaling.
source: Given the deep homology between invertebrate and vertebrate Hh signaling, the discovery that primary cilia are required for vertebrate, but not invertebrate, Hh signaling was unexpected (Huangfu et al., 2003; Huangfu and Anderson, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Primary cilia are not required for invertebrate Hh signaling.
source: Given the deep homology between invertebrate and vertebrate Hh signaling, the discovery that primary cilia are required for vertebrate, but not invertebrate, Hh signaling was unexpected (Huangfu et al., 2003; Huangfu and Anderson, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Vertebrate Hh components dynamically traffic within primary cilia in response to Hh ligand.
source: Vertebrate Hh components dynamically traffic within primary cilia in response to Hh ligand (Corbit et al., 2005; Haycraft et al., 2005; Rohatgi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: In the absence of ligand, Ptch1 is enriched on the ciliary membrane.
source: In the absence of ligand, Ptch1 is enriched on the ciliary membrane and Smo is barely detectable (Corbit et al., 2005; Rohatgi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: In the absence of ligand, Smo is barely detectable in cilia.
source: In the absence of ligand, Ptch1 is enriched on the ciliary membrane and Smo is barely detectable (Corbit et al., 2005; Rohatgi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Full length Gli proteins traffic to the ciliary tip and back to the cytoplasm before being cleaved to their repressor form.
source: Furthermore, full length Gli proteins traffic to the ciliary tip and back to the cytoplasm before being cleaved to their repressor form, which actively shuts down Hh target gene transcription in the nucleus (Kim et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2005; Wen et al., 2010; Humke et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Upon ligand stimulation, the Ptch1 receptor binds the ligand and shuttles out of cilia.
source: In contrast, upon ligand stimulation (Shh, Ihh or Dhh), the Ptch1 receptor binds the ligand and shuttles out of cilia (Rohatgi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Upon ligand stimulation, Smo is enriched in the cilium and is subsequently activated.
source: Subsequently, Smo is enriched in the cilium and is subsequently activated (Kong et al., 2019; Corbit et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Activated Smo promotes the processing of full-length Gli transcription factors into GliA.
source: Activated Smo promotes the processing of full-length Gli transcription factors into GliA, which turns on target genes (Aza-Blanc et al., 2000; Ruiz i Altaba, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Ablation of cilia results in an absence of GliA and GliR production.
source: Ablation of cilia results in an absence of GliA and GliR production, rendering the pathway inert and leading to an absence of transcriptional response (Huangfu and Anderson, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: ARL13B is a member of the ARF family of regulatory GTPases.
source: ARL13B is a member of the ARF family of regulatory GTPases and is highly enriched on the ciliary membrane (Caspary et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference and is established knowledge.

claim: In mice, a null mutation of Arl13b leads to short cilia.
source: In mice, a null mutation of Arl13b leads to short cilia and to alterations in Shh signal transduction (Caspary et al., 2007; Larkins et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: In mice, a null mutation of Arl13b leads to alterations in Shh signal transduction.
source: In mice, a null mutation of Arl13b leads to short cilia and to alterations in Shh signal transduction (Caspary et al., 2007; Larkins et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: ARL13 is ancient, predicted to be present in the last common eukaryotic ancestor.
source: ARL13 is ancient, predicted to be present in the last common eukaryotic ancestor.
evidence: This is based on evolutionary analysis cited in the manuscript.

claim: ARL13 appears to have been lost during evolution in organisms that lack cilia.
source: ARL13 appears to have been lost during evolution in organisms that lack cilia and duplicated to ARL13A and ARL13B in the urochordates, thus ARL13B is proposed to hold important clues in deciphering the links between primary cilia and vertebrate Hh signaling (Schlacht et al., 2013; Li et al., 2004; Kahn et al., 2008; East et al., 2012; Logsdon, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references on evolutionary analysis.

claim: ARL13 duplicated to ARL13A and ARL13B in the urochordates.
source: ARL13 appears to have been lost during evolution in organisms that lack cilia and duplicated to ARL13A and ARL13B in the urochordates, thus ARL13B is proposed to hold important clues in deciphering the links between primary cilia and vertebrate Hh signaling (Schlacht et al., 2013; Li et al., 2004; Kahn et al., 2008; East et al., 2012; Logsdon, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references on evolutionary analysis.

claim: ARL13B regulates endocytic traffic.
source: It regulates endocytic traffic (Barral et al., 2012), as well as the phospholipid composition of the ciliary membrane through recruitment of the lipid phosphatase INPP5E to the ciliary membrane (Humbert et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: ARL13B regulates the phospholipid composition of the ciliary membrane through recruitment of INPP5E.
source: It regulates endocytic traffic (Barral et al., 2012), as well as the phospholipid composition of the ciliary membrane through recruitment of the lipid phosphatase INPP5E to the ciliary membrane (Humbert et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: ARL13B has a conserved role as a guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) for ARL3.
source: ARL13B also has a conserved role as a guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) for ARL3, another ciliary ARF-like (ARL) protein (Gotthardt et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2016; Hanke-Gogokhia et al., 2016; Ivanova et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references and demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1.

claim: ARL13B regulates intraflagellar transport (IFT).
source: ARL13B regulates intraflagellar transport (IFT), the process that builds and maintains cilia (Cevik et al., 2010; Li et al., 2010; Nozaki et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Loss of ARL13B disrupts Shh signal transduction in at least two distinct ways: Smo enrichment in cilia occurs even in the absence of ligand and Gli activator production is diminished.
source: Critical to this work, loss of ARL13B disrupts Shh signal transduction in at least two distinct ways: Smo enrichment in cilia occurs even in the absence of ligand and Gli activator production is diminished, although Gli repressor is made normally (Caspary et al., 2007; Larkins et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: ARL13B is present in early endosomes.
source: However, ARL13B is present in early endosomes and circular dorsal ruffles on the cell surface (Barral et al., 2012; Casalou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: ARL13B is present in circular dorsal ruffles on the cell surface.
source: However, ARL13B is present in early endosomes and circular dorsal ruffles on the cell surface (Barral et al., 2012; Casalou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: A V358A variant of ARL13B does not localize to cilia as it disrupts a known VxPx cilia localization sequence.
source: We previously showed that a V358A variant of ARL13B does not localize to cilia as it disrupts a known VxPx cilia localization sequence (Higginbotham et al., 2012; Mariani et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references from prior work by the authors.

claim: Exogenous overexpression of ARL13BV358A in Arl13b null cells does not rescue cilia length.
source: Exogenous overexpression of a ARL13BV358A construct in Arl13b null cells does not rescue ARL13B-dependent phenotypes such as cilia length as well as interneuron migration and connectivity, consistent with ciliary ARL13B mediating these processes (Higginbotham et al., 2012; Mariani et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references from prior work by the authors.

claim: Overexpressed ARL13BV358A rescues the Shh-dependent ciliary enrichment of Smo in mouse embryonic fibroblasts.
source: In contrast, we found that overexpressed ARL13BV358A does rescue the Shh-dependent ciliary enrichment of Smo in mouse embryonic fibroblasts, arguing that ARL13B may function outside the cilium to regulate Smo traffic (Mariani et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference from prior work by the authors.

claim: ARL13BV358A displays normal intrinsic GTP hydrolysis activity.
source: We previously showed that mouse ARL13BV358A protein retained normal intrinsic and GAP-stimulated GTP hydrolysis activities by analyzing GST-ARL13BV358A purified from human embryonic kidney (HEK) cells (Mariani et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference from prior work by the authors.

claim: ARL13BV358A displays normal GAP-stimulated GTP hydrolysis activity.
source: We previously showed that mouse ARL13BV358A protein retained normal intrinsic and GAP-stimulated GTP hydrolysis activities by analyzing GST-ARL13BV358A purified from human embryonic kidney (HEK) cells (Mariani et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference from prior work by the authors.

claim: ARL3 spontaneously releases pre-bound GDP slowly, requiring just under 30 minutes for 50% dissociation.
source: ARL3 spontaneously releases pre-bound GDP quite slowly under the conditions in the assay, though release is linear with time, and by extrapolation requires just under 30 minutes for 50% of pre-bound [3H]GDP to dissociate (Figure 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Addition of ARL13B causes the release of 50% of GDP from ARL3 within ~10 seconds.
source: In marked contrast, addition of ARL13B under the same conditions caused the release of 50% of the GDP within ~10 seconds and close to 100% in one minute.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: There are no differences between wild type ARL13B and ARL13BV358A in GEF activity for ARL3.
source: We detected no differences between the wild type and mutant ARL13BV358A proteins in this assay, consistent with this point mutation having no effect on ARL13B GEF function (Figure 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: GEF activity is conserved within ARL13B's GTPase domain.
source: This result is consistent with GEF activity being conserved within the protein's GTPase domain while the V358A mutation is located in the C-terminal domain (Gotthardt et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on the cited reference and the structural location of the mutation.

claim: The V358A mutation is located in the C-terminal domain of ARL13B.
source: This result is consistent with GEF activity being conserved within the protein's GTPase domain while the V358A mutation is located in the C-terminal domain (Gotthardt et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on the cited reference and the structural location of the mutation.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 editing was used to change residue 358 from valine to alanine in the mouse Arl13b gene.
source: To determine the consequences of ARL13BV358A expression in vivo, we used CRISPR/Cas9 editing to change residue 358 from valine to alanine (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is described in the methods and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The heterozygous T to C base pair change for a valine to alanine change at residue 358 was confirmed by sequencing.
source: We performed sequencing of the region that flanked exon 8, using primers outside the region of the donor oligonucleotide. We confirmed the heterozygous T to C base pair change for a valine to alanine change at residue 358 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the sequencing data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Heterozygous F1 progeny were backcrossed to FVB/NJ for three generations before analysis.
source: We backcrossed heterozygous F1 progeny to FVB/NJ for three generations before analysis to minimize any off target confounds (see details in Methods).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and detailed in the methods.

claim: ARL13B-positive cilia are visible in Arl13b+/+ and Arl13bV358A/+ embryos at E10.5.
source: ARL13B-positive cilia are visible in Arl13b+/+ and Arl13bV358A/+, but not in Arl1bV358A/V358A embryos.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the immunofluorescence images in Figure 2C.

claim: ARL13B-positive cilia are not visible in Arl13bV358A/V358A embryos at E10.5.
source: ARL13B-positive cilia are visible in Arl13b+/+ and Arl13bV358A/+, but not in Arl1bV358A/V358A embryos.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the immunofluorescence images in Figure 2C.

claim: There is a ~7% reduction of ARL13B levels in Arl13bV358A/+ embryos compared to wild type.
source: We found a ~ 7% (±20%) reduction of ARL13B levels in Arl13bV358A/+ embryos and a ~ 37% (±6%) decrease of ARL13B levels in Arl13bV358A/V358A embryos, compared to WT (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the western blot quantification in Figure 2D-E.

claim: There is a ~37% decrease of ARL13B levels in Arl13bV358A/V358A embryos compared to wild type.
source: We found a ~ 7% (±20%) reduction of ARL13B levels in Arl13bV358A/+ embryos and a ~ 37% (±6%) decrease of ARL13B levels in Arl13bV358A/V358A embryos, compared to WT (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the western blot quantification in Figure 2D-E.

claim: Strong ciliary staining of ARL13B was observed with each of five antibodies in Arl13b+/+ and Arl13bV358A/+ cells.
source: By eye, we observed strong ciliary staining of ARL13B with each of the antibodies in Arl13b+/+ and Arl13bV358A/+ cells, but we were unable to identify any evidence of ARL13B staining above background within cilia in Arl13bV358A/V358A cells with any of these five antibodies (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the immunofluorescence images in Figure 3A.

claim: No evidence of ARL13B staining above background was observed within cilia in Arl13bV358A/V358A cells with any of five antibodies.
source: By eye, we observed strong ciliary staining of ARL13B with each of the antibodies in Arl13b+/+ and Arl13bV358A/+ cells, but we were unable to identify any evidence of ARL13B staining above background within cilia in Arl13bV358A/V358A cells with any of these five antibodies (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the immunofluorescence images in Figure 3A.

claim: IFT88 accumulates at ciliary tips upon ciliobrevin-D treatment in Arl13b+/+, Arl13bV358A/+, and Arl13bV358A/V358A cells.
source: We found IFT88 and Gli3 enrichment at ciliary tips in Arl13b+/+, Arl13bV358A/+ and Arl13bV358A/V358A cells upon ciliobrevin-D treatment relative to the respective DMSO-treated controls with no difference in IFT88 or Gli3 staining among the three genotypes (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the immunofluorescence data in Figure 3B.

claim: Gli3 accumulates at ciliary tips upon ciliobrevin-D treatment in Arl13b+/+, Arl13bV358A/+, and Arl13bV358A/V358A cells.
source: We found IFT88 and Gli3 enrichment at ciliary tips in Arl13b+/+, Arl13bV358A/+ and Arl13bV358A/V358A cells upon ciliobrevin-D treatment relative to the respective DMSO-treated controls with no difference in IFT88 or Gli3 staining among the three genotypes (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the immunofluorescence data in Figure 3C.

claim: About 90% of acetylated α-tubulin-positive cilia also stained for ARL13B in Arl13b+/+ and Arl13bV358A/+ cells in DMSO-treated control or ciliobrevin-D treated MEFs.
source: In Arl13b+/+ and Arl13bV358A/+ cells, we saw that about 90% of acetylated α-tubulin-positive cilia also stained for ARL13B in DMSO-treated control or ciliobrevin-D treated MEFs (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the quantification data in Figure 3D and E.

claim: No ciliary ARL13B staining was observed in Arl13bV358A/V358A MEFs in DMSO-treated control or ciliobrevin-D-treated cells using two antibodies against distinct epitopes.
source: In Arl13bV358A/V358A MEFs, we saw no ciliary ARL13B staining in DMSO-treated control or ciliobrevin-D-treated cells using two antibodies against distinct epitopes (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the quantification data in Figure 3D and E.

claim: Progeny from Arl13bV358A/+ intercrosses were observed in Mendelian proportions.
source: We observed progeny in Mendelian proportions with an average of 7.3 pups per litter, consistent with the reported FVB/NJ litter size of 7–9 (Murray et al., 2010; Table 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the breeding data in Table 1.

claim: The average litter size from Arl13bV358A/+ intercrosses was 7.3 pups.
source: We observed progeny in Mendelian proportions with an average of 7.3 pups per litter, consistent with the reported FVB/NJ litter size of 7–9 (Murray et al., 2010; Table 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the breeding data in Table 1.

claim: The Arl13bV358A allele segregated in Mendelian proportions in crosses of Arl13bV358A/V358A males to heterozygous or homozygous females.
source: To test whether homozygous mice breed normally, we crossed Arl13bV358A/V358A males to heterozygous or homozygous females. We found the Arl13bV358A allele segregated in Mendelian proportions and the litter sizes were normal indicating that Arl13bV358A does not impact viability, fertility or fecundity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the breeding data in Table 1.

claim: Litter sizes were normal in crosses involving Arl13bV358A/V358A mice.
source: To test whether homozygous mice breed normally, we crossed Arl13bV358A/V358A males to heterozygous or homozygous females. We found the Arl13bV358A allele segregated in Mendelian proportions and the litter sizes were normal indicating that Arl13bV358A does not impact viability, fertility or fecundity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the breeding data in Table 1.

claim: Arl13bV358A does not impact viability.
source: We found the Arl13bV358A allele segregated in Mendelian proportions and the litter sizes were normal indicating that Arl13bV358A does not impact viability, fertility or fecundity.
evidence: This is inferred from the Mendelian ratios and normal litter sizes shown in Table 1.

claim: Arl13bV358A does not impact fertility.
source: We found the Arl13bV358A allele segregated in Mendelian proportions and the litter sizes were normal indicating that Arl13bV358A does not impact viability, fertility or fecundity.
evidence: This is inferred from the Mendelian ratios and normal litter sizes shown in Table 1.

claim: Arl13bV358A does not impact fecundity.
source: We found the Arl13bV358A allele segregated in Mendelian proportions and the litter sizes were normal indicating that Arl13bV358A does not impact viability, fertility or fecundity.
evidence: This is inferred from the Mendelian ratios and normal litter sizes shown in Table 1.

claim: Loss of Arl13b leads to morphologically abnormal embryos.
source: Loss of Arl13b leads to morphologically abnormal embryos, lethality and neural patterning defects (Caspary et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Loss of Arl13b leads to lethality.
source: Loss of Arl13b leads to morphologically abnormal embryos, lethality and neural patterning defects (Caspary et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Loss of Arl13b leads to neural patterning defects.
source: Loss of Arl13b leads to morphologically abnormal embryos, lethality and neural patterning defects (Caspary et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: The overall morphology of Arl13bV358A/V358A embryos resembled those of Arl13b+/+ and Arl13bV358A/+ embryos at E9.5, E10.5 and E12.5.
source: We found the overall morphology of Arl13bV358A/V358A embryos resembled those of Arl13b+/+ and Arl13bV358A/+ embryos indicating that ARL13BV358A did not lead to gross morphological defects. (Figure 4A–I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the embryo images in Figure 4A-I.

claim: At E9.5, Shh is normally expressed in the notochord and the floor plate of the ventral neural tube.
source: At E9.5, Shh is normally expressed in the notochord as well as the floor plate of the ventral neural tube.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Shh expression patterns.

claim: In the Arl13bhnn/hnn neural tube, the Shh-positive columnar cells of the floor plate are absent.
source: In the Arl13bhnn/hnn (null) neural tube, the Shh-positive columnar cells of the floor plate are absent resulting in both ventral and dorsal expansion of intermediate Shh-dependent cell fates such as Olig2 (Caspary et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: No differences in Shh, Nkx2.2 or Olig2 were observed among Arl13b+/+, Arl13bV358A/+, and Arl13bV358A/V358A embryos at E9.5.
source: At E9.5 we observed no differences in Shh, Nkx2.2 or Olig2 among Arl13b+/+, Arl13bV358A/+, and Arl13bV358A/V358A embryos (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the immunofluorescence images in Figure 4A-C.

claim: Olig2, HB9 and Nkx6.1 positive cells are normally distributed in all 3 genotypes at E10.5 and E12.5.
source: We found that Olig2, HB9 and Nkx6.1 positive cells are normally distributed in all 3 genotypes at E10.5 and E12.5 (Figure 4D–I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the immunofluorescence images in Figure 4D-I.

claim: In Arl13bhnn/hnn cells, Smo is enriched in cilia in a Shh-independent manner.
source: In Arl13bhnn/hnn cells, Smo is enriched in cilia in a Shh-independent manner, which may be due to defective trafficking of Smo, as many ARL family members regulate protein trafficking (Lim et al., 2011; Larkins et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: The dorsal boundary of Smo ciliary enrichment in ventral neural progenitors was identical in Arl13b+/+, Arl13bV358A/+, and Arl13bV358A/V358A samples.
source: Smo appeared enriched normally in ventral floor plate cilia and the dorsal boundary of Smo ciliary enrichment in ventral neural progenitors was identical in Arl13b+/+, Arl13bV358A/+, and Arl13bV358A/V358A samples indicating ARL13BV358A mediates normal ciliary Smo enrichment (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the immunofluorescence images in Figure 5A.

claim: Ciliary Smo was observed in unstimulated Arl13bhnn/hnn MEFs which increased upon stimulation with Shh-conditioned media.
source: As expected in control Arl13bhnn/hnn cells, we saw ciliary Smo in unstimulated MEFs which increased upon stimulation with Shh-conditioned media (Larkins et al., 2011; Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the immunofluorescence data in Figure 5B and supported by the cited reference.

claim: Ciliary enrichment of Smo was observed upon Shh stimulation in Arl13b+/+, Arl13bV358A/+, and Arl13bV358A/V358A MEF cilia over their respective unstimulated controls.
source: In Arl13b+/+, Arl13bV358A/+, and Arl13bV358A/V358A MEF cilia, we saw ciliary enrichment of Smo upon Shh stimulation over their respective unstimulated controls (Figure 5B, left).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the immunofluorescence data in Figure 5B.

claim: No difference in Smo enrichment was found among Arl13b+/+, Arl13bV358A/+, and Arl13bV358A/V358A cell lines.
source: We found no difference in Smo enrichment among these cell lines (Figure 5B, right).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the quantification data in Figure 5B.

claim: No differences in distribution of Gli2 or Ptch1 were observed among any of the examined genotypes.

source: These results indicate that ARL13B is required in cilia for the proper localization of ARL3 and INPP5E to the cilium.

claim: Loss of Arl13b leads to defects in the percentage of ciliated MEFs.

claim: Loss of Arl13b leads to defects in cilia length.
source: Loss of Arl13b leads to defects in the percentage of ciliated MEFs and in cilia length (Caspary et al., 2007; Larkins et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: 73% of Arl13b+/+ MEFs are ciliated 24 hours after induction of ciliation by growth in low serum.
source: We found 73% (±11%) of Arl13b+/+ and 75%, (±9.1%) of Arl13bV358A/+ MEFs are ciliated, consistent with published results.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the quantification data in Figure 6A.

claim: 75% of Arl13bV358A/+ MEFs are ciliated 24 hours after induction of ciliation by growth in low serum.
source: We found 73% (±11%) of Arl13b+/+ and 75%, (±9.1%) of Arl13bV358A/+ MEFs are ciliated, consistent with published results.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the quantification data in Figure 6A.

claim: 45% of Arl13bV358A/V358A cells had cilia 24 hours after induction of ciliation by growth in low serum.
source: In contrast, we found 45% (±8.7%) of Arl13bV358A/V358A cells and 53% (±6.4%) of Arl13bhnn/hnn cells had cilia (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the quantification data in Figure 6A.

claim: 53% of Arl13bhnn/hnn cells had cilia 24 hours after induction of ciliation by growth in low serum.
source: In contrast, we found 45% (±8.7%) of Arl13bV358A/V358A cells and 53% (±6.4%) of Arl13bhnn/hnn cells had cilia (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the quantification data in Figure 6A.

claim: Arl13bV358A/V358A cells exhibit a similar deficit in percentage of ciliated MEFs as complete loss of ARL13B function.
source: Thus, Arl13bV358A/V358A cells exhibit a similar deficit in percentage of ciliated MEFs as complete loss of ARL13B function.

claim: Arl13bhnn/hnn cilia are about half as long as wild type in both embryos and MEFs.
source: Arl13bhnn/hnn cilia are about half as long as wild type in both embryos and MEFs (Caspary et al., 2007; Larkins et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: The average cilia length in Arl13b+/+ MEFs was 2.7 ± 0.8 μm.
source: We found the average cilia length in Arl13b+/+ and Arl13bV358A/+ MEFs was similar, 2.7 ± 0.8 μm and 2.6 ± 0.9 μm, respectively.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the cilia length measurements in Figure 6B.

claim: The average cilia length in Arl13bV358A/+ MEFs was 2.6 ± 0.9 μm.
source: We found the average cilia length in Arl13b+/+ and Arl13bV358A/+ MEFs was similar, 2.7 ± 0.8 μm and 2.6 ± 0.9 μm, respectively.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the cilia length measurements in Figure 6B.

claim: Arl13bV358A/V358A MEF cilia were shorter, 1.9 ± 0.7 μm.
source: However, we found Arl13bV358A/V358A MEF cilia were shorter, 1.9 ± 0.7 μm, similar to Arl13bhnn/hnn MEF cilia which were 2.15 ± 0.8 μm (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the cilia length measurements in Figure 6B.

claim: Arl13bhnn/hnn MEF cilia were 2.15 ± 0.8 μm in length.
source: However, we found Arl13bV358A/V358A MEF cilia were shorter, 1.9 ± 0.7 μm, similar to Arl13bhnn/hnn MEF cilia which were 2.15 ± 0.8 μm (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the cilia length measurements in Figure 6B.

claim: ARL13BV358A phenocopies complete loss of ARL13B for ciliation.
source: These results indicate that ARL13BV358A phenocopies complete loss of ARL13B for ciliation and cilia length, indicating these ARL13B functions require ARL13B in cilia.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar defects in ciliation rates between Arl13bV358A/V358A and Arl13bhnn/hnn cells.

claim: ARL13BV358A phenocopies complete loss of ARL13B for cilia length.
source: These results indicate that ARL13BV358A phenocopies complete loss of ARL13B for ciliation and cilia length, indicating these ARL13B functions require ARL13B in cilia.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar defects in cilia length between Arl13bV358A/V358A and Arl13bhnn/hnn cells.

claim: ARL13B functions for ciliation and cilia length require ARL13B in cilia.
source: These results indicate that ARL13BV358A phenocopies complete loss of ARL13B for ciliation and cilia length, indicating these ARL13B functions require ARL13B in cilia.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that cilia-excluded ARL13B cannot rescue ciliation or cilia length defects.

claim: ARL13B function within cilia is distinct from ARL13B function outside of cilia in a subset of activities.
source: Furthermore, these data show that ARL13B function within cilia is distinct from ARL13B function outside of cilia in a subset of activities, and that the cilia defects and Shh defects in the complete absence of ARL13B can be uncoupled.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential rescue of phenotypes by cilia-excluded ARL13B.

claim: The cilia defects and Shh defects in the complete absence of ARL13B can be uncoupled.
source: Furthermore, these data show that ARL13B function within cilia is distinct from ARL13B function outside of cilia in a subset of activities, and that the cilia defects and Shh defects in the complete absence of ARL13B can be uncoupled.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Arl13bV358A/V358A cells have cilia defects but normal Shh signaling.

claim: ARL13B's role(s) in cell ciliation can be uncoupled from ARL13B's function in regulating Shh signal transduction.
source: Here we show that ARL13B's role(s) in cell ciliation and cilia length, along with the ciliary enrichment of a subset of proteins, can be uncoupled from ARL13B's function in regulating Shh signal transduction (Figure 7).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the paper, supported by all the data presented.

claim: ARL13B's role(s) in cilia length can be uncoupled from ARL13B's function in regulating Shh signal transduction.
source: Here we show that ARL13B's role(s) in cell ciliation and cilia length, along with the ciliary enrichment of a subset of proteins, can be uncoupled from ARL13B's function in regulating Shh signal transduction (Figure 7).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the paper, supported by all the data presented.

claim: ARL13B's role in ciliary enrichment of a subset of proteins can be uncoupled from ARL13B's function in regulating Shh signal transduction.
source: Here we show that ARL13B's role(s) in cell ciliation and cilia length, along with the ciliary enrichment of a subset of proteins, can be uncoupled from ARL13B's function in regulating Shh signal transduction (Figure 7).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the paper, supported by all the data presented.

claim: This functional distinction correlates with ARL13B spatial localization to the cilium.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate this functional distinction correlates with ARL13B spatial localization to the cilium.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that functions requiring ciliary ARL13B are lost when ARL13B is excluded from cilia, while functions not requiring ciliary ARL13B are retained.

claim: ARL13B likely regulates Shh signaling from the cell body by controlling Shh component traffic to and/or from the primary cilium.
source: Based on the normal cilia trafficking of Shh components in Arl13bV358A/V358A mutants and the abnormal cilia trafficking of Shh components in the complete absence of ARL13B (Larkins et al., 2011), ARL13B likely regulates Shh signaling from the cell body by controlling Shh component traffic to and/or from the primary cilium.
evidence: This is speculated based on the data showing normal Shh signaling with cilia-excluded ARL13B and the known role of ARL13B in trafficking.

claim: Both Smo and ARL13B traffic is linked to endosomes.
source: Both Smo and ARL13B traffic is linked to endosomes providing one possible non-ciliary organelle (Barral et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2009; Milenkovic et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Arl13bhnn/hnn cells display constitutive Smo ciliary enrichment.
source: Arl13bhnn/hnn cells display constitutive Smo ciliary enrichment along with little enrichment of Gli proteins at the ciliary tip (Larkins et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Arl13bhnn/hnn cells display little enrichment of Gli proteins at the ciliary tip.
source: Arl13bhnn/hnn cells display constitutive Smo ciliary enrichment along with little enrichment of Gli proteins at the ciliary tip (Larkins et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: ARL13B regulates a step downstream of activated Smo that controls transcription factor Gli activation, but not repression.
source: ARL13B regulates a step downstream of activated Smo that controls transcription factor Gli activation, but not repression (Caspary et al., 2007; Bay et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: ARL3 residence in cilia may require that ARL3 be in (or at least cycle through) its activated, GTP-bound conformation.
source: We speculate that ARL3 residence in cilia may require that ARL3 be in (or at least cycle through) its activated, GTP-bound conformation as ARL13BV358A retains its ARL3 GEF activity, but not its cilia localization.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation that ARL3 is absent from cilia when ARL13B is excluded, despite ARL13BV358A retaining GEF activity.

claim: ARL13B is in a common protein complex with INPP5E.
source: ARL13B is in a common protein complex with INPP5E so absence of ARL13B from cilia may disrupt formation or maintenance of the complex there (Humbert et al., 2012; Nozaki et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: INPP5E regulates Shh signaling through regulation of the phosphoinositol composition of the ciliary membrane.
source: INPP5E regulates Shh signaling through regulation of the phosphoinositol composition of the ciliary membrane.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: INPP5E loss results in increased ciliary PIP2 and enrichment of Shh repressors in cilia thus resulting in lowered Shh response.
source: INPP5E loss results in increased ciliary PIP2 and enrichment of Shh repressors in cilia thus resulting in lowered Shh response (Garcia-Gonzalo et al., 2015; Chávez et al., 2015; Dyson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: In Arl13bhnn/hnn embryos and MEFs, cilia are shorter than normal.
source: In Arl13bhnn/hnn embryos and MEFs, cilia are shorter than normal and have a microtubule defect where the B-tubule of the microtubule outer doublet is open (Caspary et al., 2007; Larkins et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: In Arl13bhnn/hnn embryos and MEFs, cilia have a microtubule defect where the B-tubule of the microtubule outer doublet is open.

claim: Increased expression of ARL13B promotes cilia elongation.

evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: ARL13 functions in cilia formation and maintenance in Chlamydomonas.
source: ARL13 functions in cilia formation and maintenance in Chlamydomonas and C. elegans, neither of which have Hh signaling, consistent with the ancient role of ARL13 controlling ciliation and cilia length (Cevik et al., 2010; Cevik et al., 2013; Stolc et al., 2005; Miertzschke et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: ARL13 functions in cilia formation and maintenance in C. elegans.
source: ARL13 functions in cilia formation and maintenance in Chlamydomonas and C. elegans, neither of which have Hh signaling, consistent with the ancient role of ARL13 controlling ciliation and cilia length (Cevik et al., 2010; Cevik et al., 2013; Stolc et al., 2005; Miertzschke et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: C. elegans does not have Hh signaling.
source: ARL13 functions in cilia formation and maintenance in Chlamydomonas and C. elegans, neither of which have Hh signaling, consistent with the ancient role of ARL13 controlling ciliation and cilia length (Cevik et al., 2010; Cevik et al., 2013; Stolc et al., 2005; Miertzschke et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references and is established knowledge.

claim: Chlamydomonas does not have Hh signaling.

evidence: This is supported by the cited references and is established knowledge.

claim: ARL13B retains ARL13's ancient role in ciliogenesis.
source: Our data support ARL13B retaining ARL13's ancient role in ciliogenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ARL13B regulates cilia length and ciliation from within cilia, similar to ARL13 in other organisms.

claim: ARL13B does not work from within the cilium to regulate Shh component ciliary traffic.
source: However, our data show that ARL13B does not work from within the cilium to regulate Shh component ciliary traffic or Shh signal transduction.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that cilia-excluded ARL13B can still regulate Shh signaling normally.

claim: ARL13B does not work from within the cilium to regulate Shh signal transduction.
source: However, our data show that ARL13B does not work from within the cilium to regulate Shh component ciliary traffic or Shh signal transduction.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that cilia-excluded ARL13B can still regulate Shh signaling normally.

claim: The first known evolutionary link between cilia and Hh is in sea urchins which transduce Hh signal in developing muscle tissue via motile cilia.
source: The first known evolutionary link between cilia and Hh is in sea urchins which transduce Hh signal in developing muscle tissue via motile cilia (Warner et al., 2014; Sigg et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: The mechanistic link of cilia and Hh is limited to deuterostomes.
source: These data suggest that the mechanistic link of cilia and Hh is limited to deuterostomes and raises the question of whether the relationship of Hh and primary cilia originated near the last common ancestor of vertebrates, the urochordates.
evidence: This is inferred from evolutionary comparisons across different organisms.

claim: C. elegans have cilia yet do not possess Hh signaling as they don't have most of the genes encoding the core components of Hh signal transduction.
source: The round worm C. elegans have cilia yet do not possess Hh signaling as they don't have most of the genes encoding the core components of Hh signal transduction (The C. elegans Sequencing Consortium, 1998; Roy, 2012).

source: Curiously, a few components of Hh signaling such as fused and costal2 are in the C. elegans genome where they are functionally important for ciliogenesis (Ingham et al., 2011).

source: Additionally, C. elegans retained a Ptch1 homolog important for development and pattern formation, but no Hh or Smo (Zugasti et al., 2005; Kuwabara et al., 2000).
